core: working definition of the customer journey: the full path a customer travels with a brand, from first learning it exists through considering, buying, and what happens after the purchase — anchored on HubSpot's definition (the series of interactions a customer has with a brand or product as they become aware of a problem and make a purchase decision) and extended past the sale by OpenStax's post-purchase evaluation stage

the four stages named with one line and an original example each: awareness, consideration, decision, loyalty — presented as a common teaching simplification grounded in OpenStax's documented five-step consumer decision process
touchpoints: every moment the customer comes into direct contact with the brand — NN/g's interaction-based definition, with an original Harbor Books example
the honest note: the journey is not linear — customers loop back and skip stages (HubSpot; McKinsey's consumer decision journey)
mapping the journey: laying out stages and touchpoints as a visualization of the process a person goes through (NN/g Journey Mapping 101; IxDF) — a research-based practice

the connection to the mix: each P shapes the journey — promotion creates awareness, product shapes evaluation, price shapes comparison, place shapes where touchpoints happen (marketing-mix is a sibling topic, referenced only)
the honest framing: the journey is the customer's, not the marketer's — companies influence touchpoints but do not control the path
supporting: the distinction between the customer journey (specific to one brand, includes post-purchase) and the buyer's journey (generic awareness-consideration-decision path), per HubSpot
the five-step consumer decision process from OpenStax (need recognition, information search, evaluation of alternatives, purchase decision, post-purchase evaluation) as the skeleton of the journey
channels versus touchpoints: channels are methods of communication or service delivery such as a website or physical store (NN/g)
the loyalty loop: post-purchase experience feeds loyalty and advocacy (McKinsey)
brand loyalty as repeat purchase and advocacy (OpenStax section 9.6)
stage counts vary by framework (three, four, five, or seven stages); the four-stage account used here is a simplification, not a law
outOfScope: conversion measurement and optimization — sibling topic marketing:foundations:conversion owns it
the psychology of why people buy — sibling topic marketing:foundations:consumer-behavior owns it; only the decision-process skeleton is borrowed here
measuring journeys with data, metrics, and attribution — sibling topic marketing:foundations:marketing-analytics owns it
market research methods (surveys, interviews, sampling) — sibling topic marketing:foundations:market-research owns them; referenced only as the source of journey-mapping data
the four Ps in depth — sibling topic marketing:foundations:marketing-mix owns them; only the journey connection is made here

claims.claim: The customer journey is the series of interactions a customer has with a brand or product as they become aware of a problem and make a purchase decision; the buyer's journey is the generic three-stage path (awareness, consideration, decision) any shopper takes, while the customer journey is the specific path with one brand.

The consumer decision process runs through five steps — need recognition, information search, evaluation of alternatives, purchase decision, and post-purchase evaluation — and the buying process continues after the sale, when the customer judges the purchase against expectations and may experience cognitive dissonance (buyer's remorse).
Touchpoints are the moments when the customer actually interacts with the company, while channels are the methods of communication or service delivery such as a website or a physical store.
Most customer journeys are not linear: buyers move back and forth through a cyclical, multi-channel journey with many touchpoints.

The traditional marketing funnel fails to capture all the touch points and key buying factors in a digital market full of product choices; the purchase environment is less linear than the funnel suggests, and post-purchase experience feeds a loyalty loop of repeat buying and advocacy.

A journey map is a visualization of the process a person goes through to accomplish a goal; journey maps are research-based visual representations giving a 360-degree view of engagement over time and across channels, used to identify pain points and opportunities.
Loyal customers purchase again and advocate for the brand; brand loyalty ranges from switchers to hard-core loyals.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many stages does the customer journey have?
positions: HubSpot's buyer's journey uses three stages: awareness, consideration, decision.
OpenStax's Principles of Marketing documents a five-step consumer decision process: need recognition, information search, evaluation of alternatives, purchase decision, post-purchase evaluation.
Many teaching accounts, including this lesson, use four stages: awareness, consideration, decision, loyalty.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the four-stage account as a common simplification, names the other framings, and grounds the stages in OpenStax's documented five-step process; learners are told stage counts vary by framework.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Are 'customer journey' and 'buyer's journey' the same thing?
positions: HubSpot distinguishes the buyer's journey (the generic path to a purchase) from the customer journey (the specific path with one brand, including post-purchase).
Everyday usage often treats the two terms interchangeably.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows HubSpot's distinction in one sentence and otherwise uses 'customer journey' as the umbrella term for the full path a customer travels with a brand.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, Section 3.3: The Consumer Purchasing Decision Process
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A backbone; re-verified via Internet Archive capture dated 2023-02-03. Supports: the five-step consumer decision process — need recognition (sensing a difference between actual and desired state), information search (heightened attention versus active search, including asking friends and family), evaluation of alternatives (products viewed as bundles of attributes), purchase decision, and post-purchase evaluation (satisfaction versus dissatisfaction; cognitive dissonance, or buyer's remorse, leading customers to seek confirming information). Concepts adapted into original prose.
